Oral medicine and dentistry · published research

Oral mucosal necrosis

Uncontrolled reports describe reduced pain and analgesic use followed by healing over three to six weeks, but comparative efficacy is unknown.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Uncontrolled reports describe reduced pain and analgesic use followed by healing over three to six weeks, but comparative efficacy is unknown.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Oral > Oral mucosal necrosis category contains two unique human publications: one case report and one three-case series. Both concern persistent radiation-associated oral or oropharyngeal ulceration. No controlled trial, animal study, or laboratory record was identified. These reports describe four cases, not four independent clinical studies.

Human and clinical evidence

In the French case report, pain had decreased and daily analgesic use had fallen by two weeks; clinical improvement was noted by week three, and the lesion was fully healed after six weeks of PBM (de Bataille et al. 2017). A United States case series described three patients with persistent ulceration after head and neck cancer treatment. The authors reported rapid resolution of lesions and symptoms during a three-to-six-week course (Epstein et al. 2016). Neither publication had a comparison group, and patients received care in a specialized post-cancer setting.

Animal evidence

No relevant animal evidence was identified for radiation-associated mucosal necrosis.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo experiment was identified in the exact category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The case report used a 660-nm red laser at 150 mW with a reported fluence of 4 J/cm², twice weekly for six weeks. In the case series, intraoral 660-nm laser treatment was combined with extraoral red and near-infrared LED application at 660 and 850 nm, twice weekly. The different delivery routes, sources, and treatment schedules make the two reports difficult to compare directly.

Interpretation

These observations show that pain relief and wound closure occurred during PBM treatment in several patients. They do not establish how outcomes would have changed with standard care alone, nor do they quantify recurrence or long-term tissue effects.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for pain relief or healing of radiation-associated oral mucosal necrosis because evidence comes from uncontrolled reports
Publications and records2 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two publications describe four people in total, with no control group and no independent replication in a trial. The reports provide useful clinical observations but cannot show how much healing or pain change was caused by PBM. Comparative studies should measure ulcer closure, pain, analgesic use, and recurrence.
